Hotels: only 8% of hoteliers see more than three quarters of guests return

Getting a guest to come back is every hotelier's dream. It costs less than attracting a new one, and it shows the experience truly worked. Yet the available data shows that returning guests remain the exception rather than the rule.

A 2014 survey by Tripadvisor and Ipsos of 14,083 hoteliers worldwide asked them what share of their guests had come back for another stay. The answers are old, as we point out from the start, but they describe a reality that more recent data on the sector does not contradict.

What the 2014 survey said

38% of hoteliers surveyed said that 25% or fewer of their guests had returned for another stay. 35% put that share between 26 and 50%. 17% between 51 and 75%. And only 8% of hoteliers saw more than three quarters of their guests return.

In other words, nearly three quarters of properties (73%) saw at most half of their guests come back. The source notes that several answers were possible, which is why the total does not add up to exactly 100%.

These figures date from July 2014. They do not measure today's situation property by property, but they give an order of magnitude for how hard the sector finds loyalty.

Treat them as a historical benchmark, not as a current measurement.

Consistent with retention data

This matches other data. According to CustomerGauge, NPS Benchmarks and MIT CISR, the customer retention rate in hospitality, travel and restaurants was 55% in 2018, the lowest of all industries studied. We covered that ranking in our article on customer retention by industry.

The market itself is not short of customers. According to Statista's Hotels dossier, worldwide hotel segment revenue is estimated at $362.74 billion in 2025. The challenge is not attracting people; it is making them want to come back.

Why guests do not come back

Part of it is natural: many travelers never return to the same city. But another part comes down to the experience itself. A noisy room, a distant welcome, a disappointing breakfast, a poorly explained bill: each of these details is enough to steer the next booking elsewhere.

Guests talk about these details. They write them in online reviews, mention them in end-of-stay surveys, raise them in an email or on the phone. The problem is not a lack of information, but the difficulty of using hundreds of messages scattered across several platforms.

Booking platforms also matter. According to Statista's Hotels dossier, online channels accounted for 77% of worldwide hotel revenue in 2024. Before booking again, many guests reread reviews, including those about their own past stays.

Turning reviews into an action plan

Automatic language analysis can read all of this feedback and organize it by theme: cleanliness, noise, bedding, welcome, food, value for money. For each theme, it measures the tone of comments and how it changes over time.

A hotel manager then knows, every week, which topics drag satisfaction down and which are improving. A hotel group can compare its properties and spot where a problem keeps recurring. Our hospitality and restaurants page describes these uses.

The analysis relies on models such as Mistral, BERT, Llama, GPT or Claude depending on the case, and data stays hosted in France.

The point is not to replace the judgment of hotel teams, who know their property best, but to give them a complete and up-to-date picture instead of the few reviews they happen to read.

Measuring what brings guests back

Loyalty cannot be decreed; it is built by fixing what disappoints and reinforcing what pleases. Positive reviews are as valuable as negative ones: they show what loyal guests appreciate and what must be preserved.

By tracking both the return rate and the content of guest feedback, a hotelier can link actions to their effects. That is what it takes to one day join the 8% who see most of their guests come back.

One last piece of advice: reply to reviews, positive and negative. Guests who see their comment taken into account are more willing to give a second chance, and future guests read those replies carefully.

What this means for you

In hospitality, returning guests are the exception. The reasons they do not come back are written in your reviews and messages. custovox.ai reads all of them, property by property, to show you what to fix first and what to preserve.
